question: Where did my atoms come from?
teaser: Trace the oxygen and carbon in your body back through the periodic table, the stars and the first minutes of the universe.

stops.title: What you are made of, by element
text: About 99 percent of your body's mass is just six elements: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus.
Each atom of those has a history that began long before you. The question is where each kind was made.
stops.notice: Open the card and look at the main elements it lists.

stops.title: One atom of oxygen
text: This is an oxygen atom. What makes it oxygen, and not carbon or iron, is the number of protons in its nucleus: eight.
Atoms of the same element are identical in the ways that matter, whether they are in your breath, in a rock or in a star.
stops.model: A computed model of the electron cloud. Each dot marks one place an electron could be found.
stops.notice: Try "Cut away a quarter" to see inside the cloud. The nucleus is at its true size, so it is too small to see at this zoom.

stops.title: The table of elements
text: Every kind of atom found in nature, and some made in laboratories, is in this table, in order of the number of protons. There are 118 elements in it.
Only a few of them were made in the first minutes of the universe. All the rest had to be made later, and somewhere else.
stops.notice: Press the button at the top that says "Element: Oxygen (O) · periodic table" to open the table. Choose "Colour by" and try "Year discovered". Close it to come back to the trail.

stops.title: A star making helium
text: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release energy. This is how stars turn one element into another. Late in its life the Sun will make carbon and oxygen too, and bigger stars go on to build elements up as far as iron.
stops.model: The core's temperature and density come from a standard solar model, not from direct measurement.
stops.notice: The core is where a star's atoms are changed. Outside the core it is too cool for fusion.

stops.title: Stars and their deaths
text: Massive stars forge elements from carbon up to iron, and their supernova explosions throw the new atoms, including much of the oxygen, out into space. Elements heavier than iron come by two routes: a slow one inside old giant stars, and a rapid one in violent events such as the collision of neutron stars. Later stars and planets form from that gas, so the carbon and oxygen in you were made in earlier stars before the Sun was born.
stops.model: The stars shown are real, at catalogue positions. The supernovae themselves are not drawn.
stops.notice: Read the card. It says how much of the heaviest elements comes from mergers is still debated.

deeper.label: White dwarfs, supernovae and neutron stars

stops.title: The first nuclei and atoms
text: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state. Protons formed within the first second, and in the first few minutes some of them fused into the nuclei of helium, with traces of deuterium and lithium. About 380,000 years later it had cooled enough for the first whole atoms to form. By mass, the ordinary matter was then about 74 percent hydrogen and 24 percent helium.
stops.model: The glowing shell and its patterns are illustrations, not the measured map of the early universe.
stops.notice: The hydrogen nuclei in the water in you formed in the first second of the universe. The oxygen in it came from stars.

answer: The hydrogen in you was made in the Big Bang, and most of the heavier atoms, such as the carbon and oxygen, were made inside stars and thrown into space when they died.
unknown: How much of the heaviest elements, such as gold, comes from neutron star mergers and how much from other kinds of supernova is still debated, and the lithium made in the Big Bang is about three times less than predicted.
